A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same event-inference benchmark and retain the same underlying datasets. Their main text, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable matching across revisions and relocations.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of language models on sports and four open-domain datasets, including context ablations, sequence-length analyses, and time-series similarity experiments.

after.justification: V2 retains those original evaluations and adds post-training experiments, a time-series replacement ablation, reasoning-failure analyses, and win-probability calibration results.

M1.justification: V2 introduces a training procedure absent from v1: warm up Qwen2.5 1.5B using correct reasoning traces from DS-R1-distill-Qwen-32B, then apply GRPO with correctness and format rewards (Section 4.2, Appendix B.2). The original multiple-choice inference task and CoT prompting approach remain.

E1.justification: NBA, NFL, Bitcoin, trade, influenza, and gasoline coverage is retained. V2 adds a limited mismatched-input scenario by replacing the supplied sports time series with a series from another game (Section 4.3, Table 3). Post-training uses the existing sports domains.

E2.justification: V2 adds o1 to the existing accuracy comparison and introduces an untrained Qwen2.5 1.5B reference in the new post-training comparison. The original models and all eleven open-domain comparators remain; the fuller DeepSeek names identify existing distilled models.

E3.justification: V2 adds a controlled four-condition training experiment, using training games distinct from test games, correct teacher traces for warm-up, and 7,500 RL question-answer pairs per sport. New protocols also cover replacement inputs, token-binned reasoning analysis, and calibration using game-start probabilities and outcomes. The existing benchmark evaluation sizes are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses test the separate contributions of warm-up and RL, dependence on correctly paired time series, failures associated with short or long reasoning, and ESPN probability calibration. These substantially expand diagnostic evidence. The original event-count and similarity analyses remain, including the event-count study moved to Appendix B.3.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The 10,000-pair bootstrapped distance analysis is retained from v1 Appendix A.4 in v2 Appendix B.4. The new diagnostic plots report descriptive values without introducing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Existing model accuracy bars, context-table entries, and open-domain scores are unchanged. V2 adds substantial results: Table 2 reports o1 at 166/200 NBA and 151/200 NFL correct, and Qwen2.5 1.5B with warm-up plus RL at 151/200 and 88/200, versus 11/200 and 29/200 before training. Replacement, failure-analysis, and calibration findings are also new. V1's model-specific CoT format-failure counts are omitted.

T1.justification: The time-series and event-sequence definitions, timestamp-alignment assumptions, and normalized Euclidean-distance formulation are unchanged. V2 adds no formal theorem, proof, or mathematical derivation for its post-training procedure.

C1.justification: V2 expands the central contribution from benchmarking existing models to demonstrating post-training improvements. Its abstract, introduction, and conclusion newly claim that trained Qwen2.5 1.5B surpasses its teacher and ranks second only to o1. O1 also replaces the distilled DeepSeek model as the reported overall benchmark leader.

C2.justification: Appendix B.2 newly interprets warm-up as supplying reasoning capabilities that RL can reinforce. Appendix C adds substantive explanations involving rushed reasoning, overthinking, and excessive self-reflection. Appendix E interprets game-start calibration as evidence of agreement between ESPN predictions and outcomes. V1 mainly discusses successful reasoning and contextual effects.

D1.justification: V2 documents teacher-sample collection and filtering, separation of training and test games, training-data quantities, a post-training prompt, reward types and maxima, the open-r1 framework, and eight H200 GPUs. These substantially extend v1's implementation information, which primarily identifies A100 evaluation hardware and refers readers to the repository. Overall code/data access statements and licensing remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds literature supporting post-training and reasoning-failure interpretations, including DeepSeekMath, s1, Open R1, VLM-R1, and studies of R1 behavior, plus o1 and BIG-bench references. The central positioning against existing time-series and event-reasoning benchmarks in Section 2 and Table 1 remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, dataset description, and experimental narrative are substantially revised around post-training. The event-count study moves from the main text into a reorganized experimental-results appendix; the reasoning discussion becomes separate success and failure subsections. The title and DeepSeek terminology are also revised.

P2.justification: V2 adds the training-comparison table, a replacement-ablation column, training curves, token-analysis and calibration plots, a training-prompt display, and failure examples. It splits the original NBA/NFL accuracy figure, relocates NFL results to the appendix, and introduces a compact open-domain table while retaining the full table in the appendix.

improvement.justification: The warm-up/RL controls, replacement ablation, and game-start calibration provide useful evidence about trainability, dependence on paired inputs, and data quality. However, the headline 'second only to o1' claim is broader than Table 2's selected comparison, which omits the teacher's CoT setting shown elsewhere. Section 6 also still describes training as future work. These reporting inconsistencies temper the empirical benefits, supporting a limited net improvement.
